concepts.name: The Everything Issue (a NAIRA cover)
concepts.idea: The most-clicked hoops photo becomes the cover of a magazine with NAIRA as its masthead: 'The Everything Issue'. Where a magazine prints its cover price, the dateline prints the price of the whole shop, ₹599 to ₹2,399. A vertical credit like a photo credit says 'On the cover: Woven Gold Hoops, ₹1,199', and the cover line says what is inside: rings, earrings, necklaces, bracelets.
concepts.why_beautiful: H08 is the calmest photo in the pool: two braided hoops on half a persimmon on peach linen, with soft linen above and below. Printed full bleed at 1.0x, that linen becomes the cover paper, so no panel or gradient is needed. A real cover hierarchy (masthead, hairline dateline, italic issue title, a tiny rotated credit, one cover line) in ink only leaves the gold of the hoops and the orange of the persimmon as the only colour. About 9% of the frame is type.
concepts.why_clicks: The photo is proven: Woven Gold Hoops ads ran 5.81% ('Woven, not cast.') and 6.08% CTR, and the hoops are 'most loved' on the site. The line is a quiet editorial turn. 'The Everything Issue' promises a whole magazine of her jewellery, and the cover-price joke (₹599 to ₹2,399 where ₹150 usually sits) rewards a second look. To find out what is inside, she has to open it.
concepts.shop_all_logic: A cover only ever opens an issue. The issue is the whole shop: the dateline gives the full range ₹599 to ₹2,399, the cover line names all four categories, and the hoops are credited as just the cover star.

concepts.name: Sold. The rest are on view.
concepts.idea: A gallery wall in deep anaar red. On it, the account's best-converting photo, the ruby bracelet with pomegranate, hangs in a thin gilt frame with a mishri-white mat. Beside it is a museum label with a red dot and the word Sold. Above it, the wall vinyl reads: 'Sold. The rest are on view.' The bracelet really is sold out, and saying so plainly turns that into the invitation.
concepts.why_beautiful: A real picture-gallery palette sampled from the photo: wall #4A1A20 (the deepest aril shadow in H18, softened), mat #F6EFE6, gilt keyline from the bracelet's gold (#9A6B2F to #C9A15B), and the red dot as the only spot of bright colour. There is one framed object with a weighted bottom mat and a soft gallery shadow, and the label sits on the frame's bottom line, like a museum hang. Lots of quiet wall. Everything sits on one left axis (x 96) and one right axis (x 1008).
concepts.why_clicks: H18 is the best-converting single photo in the account (E2 fruit plate: 4.32% CTR on 20,253 impressions, 24 purchases at 2.27x), so people who already clicked it will recognise it. Opening an ad with 'Sold.' is unexpected and honest. It creates desire without fake urgency, and 'The rest are on view.' turns the disappointment into curiosity about what is still there.
concepts.shop_all_logic: The hero cannot be bought, by design. The only action left is the rest of the collection, and the breadth line names it: rings, earrings, necklaces, bracelets, ₹599 to ₹2,399. It follows the pool.json rule for H18: Sold said plainly with a red dot, no price, no 'last one', and the click goes to the rest of the shop.

concepts.name: Slip, model's own.
concepts.idea: A fashion-magazine page: two on-model listing photos side by side, with the fashion credit every stylist writes, 'Slip, model’s own.', turned into the headline. The joke is that the mustard slip in every Naira photo is the one thing she cannot buy. The second line closes it: 'Everything else, from ₹599.'
concepts.why_beautiful: A strict diptych: two equal portrait tiles (444 wide each, 48px gutter) on Naira cream paper, both cropped from just under the nose down to the slip, so the same model, light and mustard rhyme across the gutter. The type is a real magazine page: italic headline, a gold second line, credits in small italics under each plate, and a hairline foot with the categories and the logo. The warm beige of the listing photos and the gold accent are the only colours.
concepts.why_clicks: These are the store's own on-model listing photos, which the Bestsellers catalogue carousel is built on: 5.73% CTR with 43 purchases at 2.67x in the last 14 days, the account's best purchase driver. Both pieces are 'most loved' on the site (Bold Nocturne Chain, Prism Rivière Bracelet). The headline is a fashion-insider wink a stylish 28-year-old will get, and the turn ('Everything else, from ₹599.') is the click.
concepts.shop_all_logic: The headline rules out one thing (the slip), so the line under it hands her everything else: the whole collection from ₹599. The footer names all four categories. The two credits show a necklace and a bracelet at two price points, as examples of the range and not the point.

concepts.name: Come in.
concepts.idea: An exhibition poster for the whole collection, built on the rangoli-at-the-threshold photo. A rangoli is drawn at the door to welcome people in, so the poster's title is simply 'Come in.' The info block reads like an exhibition's: what is on, the range, 'Open all night', and 'Admission free. Shipping too.'
concepts.why_beautiful: A Swiss-editorial poster: a cream band with one enormous Cormorant title, a hairline, and two quiet rows of type on a strict grid. Below it, the photo runs full bleed at 1.0x as two-thirds of the poster: the teak threshold, a wrist wearing the Prism Rivière, and the aqua, pink and yellow rangoli, the only colours in the frame. The hard line between paper and photo makes it read like a printed poster, not an overlay.
concepts.why_clicks: H03 was built on the 6.10% CTR 'Rangoli, in a line.' winner and shows the most-loved Prism Rivière Bracelet. It follows the account's strongest lesson: a familiar Indian thing turned into a line. Here the meaning of rangoli at the door becomes the invitation. 'Admission free. Shipping too.' is a small wry payoff that carries a true offer (free insured shipping) without shouting a discount.
concepts.shop_all_logic: 'Come in.' invites her to the whole house, not one object. The first info row names all four categories and the full range ₹599 to ₹2,399, and the poster frames the shop as an exhibition you walk into and browse.

concepts.name: Contents (the page numbers are prices)
concepts.idea: The ruby necklace with anaar becomes the frontispiece of a book whose contents page sits on the plaster wall above it. The chapters are the Indian things Naira's best ads are made of (Anaar, Rangoli, Pheni), and the folio numbers are their prices; the last chapter is 'Everything else ... from 599'. A small footnote gives the game away: 'Page numbers are prices.'
concepts.why_beautiful: H06 already has a book's proportions: about 700px of calm blush wall above a neck form wearing the ruby necklace, with a halved pomegranate and loose arils below. The contents page is set into that wall like a printed page, with no panel: a running head (logo left, tracked caps right), a hairline, an italic 'Contents', and four entries with gold lower-case roman numerals, fine dot leaders and old-style figures in Cormorant. The photo stays at 1.0x and untouched. The only colours are blush, ink, a little gold and the ruby.
concepts.why_clicks: H06 succeeds 'Anaar, pre-peeled.' (5.49% CTR, 15 sales at 3.63x; the ruby line has 24 purchases lifetime), and Anaar, Rangoli and Pheni are names Naira's audience has already clicked on (6.10% 'Rangoli, in a line.', 4.32% 'Finer than pheni.'). The surprise is quiet. A contents page whose page numbers turn out to be prices invites a second read, and 'Rangoli 2,399' and 'Pheni 1,399' make her curious what those chapters look like.
concepts.shop_all_logic: A contents page is the whole book by definition. Three chapters are a curated edit across a necklace, a bracelet and a cuff, and the fourth, 'Everything else ... from 599', opens the rest of the collection with the true floor price.

concepts.name: Set in gold tone. (the colophon)
concepts.idea: The colophon, the small note at the back of a fine book that says what it was set in and printed on, written for Naira. 'Set in gold tone.' is both a typographer's phrase and a jeweller's. The note under it describes the whole collection as an edition: some copies in silver tone, issued as rings, earrings, necklaces and bracelets, ₹599 to ₹2,399, each copy bound in the Naira gift box.
concepts.why_beautiful: H16 is stationery already: a deckle-edged envelope, a gold wax seal and the knot bangle on pink plaster, so the seal works as the printer's device. The colophon is centred on the photo's own calm plaster below the object, the way a colophon sits alone at the foot of the last page: a tracked gold label, an italic line, three or four lines of quiet roman type. In the Story it ends with the logo as the publisher's mark. Symmetrical, airy, ink and gold only.
concepts.why_clicks: The photo is proven ('Sealed with a kiss.' 3.90% CTR) and the knot bangle is a high-stock gold piece. No jewellery brand in India runs a colophon. The headline works plainly for anyone ('set in gold tone' sounds like jewellery) and rewards anyone who notices the book joke. The body slips in true reasons to click (the full range, the gift box, free insured shipping) without a single shouted offer.
concepts.shop_all_logic: A colophon describes the whole edition, not one copy, so every line is about the collection: both tones, all four categories, the full price range, the gift box every piece arrives in, and (in the Story) free insured delivery in 3-5 working days.

concepts.name: Someone finished the anaar
concepts.idea: The account's best-converting photo, the sold-out ruby bracelet with a halved pomegranate, runs full bleed and openly admits the bracelet is gone. It works like the sold-out swatch on a product page: one ruby chip with a fine diagonal line through it, labelled plainly. The wry line borrows a household moment ('Someone finished the anaar.') and the answer ('Plenty of colour left, though.') sends people to the rest of the shop. No jewellery brand in India runs an ad that leads with a sold-out piece and says so.
concepts.why_beautiful: One photo, untouched, covers the frame: ruby, blush plaster and gold tone, with the jewel close to the lower power point and the top-left third left as quiet plaster for the type. The only device is one 56px swatch sampled from the stones (#91293C) with a hairline strike, which is the frame's single accent. The type is a three-line Cormorant italic stack, a small Jost label and one hairline rule. The only colours on the page come from the photo.
concepts.why_clicks: H18 (E2 fruit plate) is the best-converting single photo in the account: 4.32% CTR on 20,253 impressions and 24 purchases at 2.27x. The anaar idea it descends from, 'Anaar, pre-peeled.', ran at 5.49% CTR with 15 sales at 3.63x. The headline makes people stop because a jewellery ad seems to be talking about fruit. The struck swatch explains the joke in a second, and honesty about a sell-out reads as proof that people buy, with no fake urgency.
concepts.shop_all_logic: The hero cannot be bought, so the only action left is the rest of the shop. 'Plenty of colour left' invites browsing by colour, and the whisper lists all four categories and the starting price. The person clicks to see what is still in.

'Elaichi, in a row.' turns the bracelet into cardamom lined up, the same move as the 6.10% winner 'Rangoli, in a line.' A running head ('Rhymes · No. 1') and the line 'Also rhyming: anaar, mishri, rangoli.' make it one rhyme out of a collection of them.
concepts.why_beautiful: A disciplined diptych: two equal portrait panels with a 40px gutter, cut from the same plaster so they read as one surface split in two. The ground is a flat cardamom olive (#6E6627) sampled from the pods, so the whole page is olive, cream and emerald, with one gold hairline sampled from the clasp. An olive ground is a colour nobody else is using in the feed. 'Also rhyming' raises a question the shop answers: which pieces rhyme with anaar, mishri and rangoli?

concepts.name: Colours, by their pet names (shade card)
concepts.idea: A paint-shop shade card for jewellery. A tall window holds the Prism Rivière bracelet on its rangoli stripes. Beside it is a strip of five flat chips sampled from five real pieces, each given its Indian pet name ('ghar ka naam'): ruby red is Anaar, gold tone is Kesar, clear is Mishri, lilac is Jamuni, emerald green is Elaichi. The headline 'Colours, by their pet names.' gives the system a warm, family logic. Indian jewellery ads do not give their stone colours family pet names on a shade card.
concepts.why_beautiful: An asymmetric two-column grid: one dominant photo (480x920) and a vertical paint strip (400x920) that touch at the same top and bottom lines, separated by 2px paper seams. The flat chips are the frame's quiet area, and every colour is sampled from a pool photo, not invented. Pet names are set in Cormorant italic, formal names in tracked Jost caps, with one paper name tab on the window, like the tab on a paint card. Paper ground, generous margins, and the only words are names.
concepts.why_clicks: The window is H02, the 6.10% CTR 'Rangoli, in a line.' Story photo. The chips name proven pieces: Woven Gold Hoops (ads at 5.81-6.08%), the ruby Baguette Tennis Necklace (successor to 'Anaar, pre-peeled.' at 5.49%), and the Edition Two tennis set (catalogue 4.37%, 41 purchases). The click comes from delight and curiosity: people recognise 'Elaichi' and 'Mishri', want to see which piece is 'Jamuni', and treat the card as a menu.
concepts.shop_all_logic: Each chip is a different piece in a different category (necklace, hoops, bracelet, huggies, ring, plus the bracelet in the window), so the card is effectively a colour index of the shop. The footer says every shade is in the shop and gives the starting price.

concepts.why_beautiful: Every tone on the page is gold, cream or umber: a ground sampled from the close-ups' plinth backdrop (#F4EBE1), umber type sampled from the gold's shadow side (#3D2A17), and gold hairlines and keylines (#C9A15B). It is a strict two-column grid, with equal 640x300 panels, equal gaps, and labels aligned to each panel's top edge. The three craft words read down the left like a poem. Because the macros come from one catalogue shoot (the same plaster plinth and the same light), the column reads as one set.
concepts.why_clicks: The craft-truth grammar is the account's top performer: 'Poured, not made.' 7.25% and 'Woven, not cast.' 5.81%. Here it becomes a three-beat rhythm with a wry fourth beat. The pieces are proven: Bold Nocturne Chain is 'Most loved' on the site, and Kiss Knot Bangle ran 'Sealed with a kiss.' at 3.90%. The macros come from the listing close-up set behind the catalogue ads.

concepts.idea: A stylist's colour-pairing card built from the on-model photo itself: the model's mustard (haldi) slip strap and her sky-blue (aasmani) heart drop, introduced to each other. Two swatch circles sampled from the photo sit beside the headline, and the line 'Whatever you're wearing, the collection has its match.' turns one pairing into a reason to browse the whole shop. Colour-combination cards are a fashion format, and no Indian jewellery brand pairs a piece with the outfit already in its photo.
concepts.why_beautiful: One large on-model crop (920x860) carries the frame: warm skin, dark hair, the aqua heart on the left power point, and the mustard strap cutting across the lower left. Below it is a calm band on a ground sampled from the photo's wall (#F6E9DC), with a Cormorant italic headline, two swatch circles and one hairline. The two swatches are the only added colour, and both come from the photo.
concepts.why_clicks: The on-model listing set is the account's best purchase driver: the Bestsellers carousel built on these photos runs at 5.73% CTR with 43 purchases at 2.67x. Naming colours as Indian things is the house formula behind 6.10% ('Rangoli, in a line.') and 6.21% ('Almost edible.'). Colour-pairing advice is something a stylish 28-year-old already saves, and this is the first time a jewellery ad hands it to her.
concepts.shop_all_logic: The pairing is the example, and the promise is general: whatever you are wearing, a piece in the collection matches it. That sends people to browse by colour across all categories from ₹599, not to buy the one earring.

concepts.name: Subtitled: Where’s the rest?
concepts.idea: A film still. The man’s open palm offering the Woven Gold Hoops (H07) is letterboxed in black like a scene from a slow, warm, late-night film, and the dialogue runs as subtitles: “– I got you these. / – Cute. Where’s the rest?” In the Story it plays as shot and reverse shot: his palm with the hoops, then her hand, already wearing the Cushion Halo Ring, with her reply. The click is the reply: the rest is the whole shop.
concepts.why_beautiful: One image, cropped to widescreen and set on deep black, does all the work. The black bars are the air, the gold bokeh and hoops glow against them, and the only type is two quiet lines of serif subtitles and a gold whisper. Restrained, cinematic and expensive-looking, nothing like a jewellery ad.
concepts.why_clicks: H07 is the Woven Gold Hoops picture, and Woven Gold Hoops ads ran at 6.08% (‘It has been rolling for miles.’) and 5.81% (‘Woven, not cast.’) CTR. It is also a site ‘most loved’ piece. H13 (Diwali 10 ad 06) shows the Cushion Halo Ring in the same warm card-night light. Subtitles look native to a feed full of video, so people read them by reflex. ‘Where’s the rest?’ is a wry, sharp-friend reply that asks the Shop All question for the viewer. No jewellery brand in India runs a subtitled film still.
concepts.shop_all_logic: The line explicitly turns away from the single gift toward ‘the rest’, and the whisper names it: rings, earrings, necklaces, bracelets, ₹599 to ₹2,399. The hoops (and in the Story the ring) are only the opening scene; tapping goes to the rest.

concepts.name: One link leads to another
concepts.idea: An extreme macro of a single pavé link from the Bold Nocturne Chain fills the frame, glowing on cream. The headline is an old saying that is literally true of a chain and of a good shop: “One link leads to another.” Start with this one and the rest of the collection follows.
concepts.why_beautiful: It is pure object photography: one link, big, sharp, warm gold and white sparkle on a soft cream ground with long shadows. The photo’s own empty top-left corner becomes the page for two lines of Cormorant (roman, then italic), and there are no devices at all. It reads like a jewellery monograph cover.
concepts.why_clicks: Bold Nocturne Chain is one of the site’s three ‘most loved’ pieces. The close-up comes from the store’s own listing set (worn/), the set the Bestsellers catalogue carousel is built on (5.73% CTR, 43 purchases at 2.67x in 14 days, the account’s best purchase driver). Macro sparkle at this scale is the thumb-stop. The line is a familiar idiom with a quiet double meaning (a chain link, and a tap that opens the shop), a cousin of the ‘X, not Y’ craft truths that won.
concepts.shop_all_logic: The headline frames the hero as the first link in a chain of discoveries, and the breadth line names what follows: rings, earrings, necklaces, bracelets, ₹599 to ₹2,399. The chain is credited with its price as just one piece of ‘the whole collection’.

concepts.name: Gone to a good home
concepts.idea: The account’s best-converting photo, the ruby tennis bracelet on the anaar plate, is hung as a single framed print on a blush plaster wall with a museum label and a small red ‘SOLD’ dot. The headline is an affectionate Indian-English phrase: “Gone to a good home.” The bracelet is honestly sold out, and the rest of the collection is still on view.
concepts.why_beautiful: A single passe-partout print floats on a wall sampled from the photo’s own blush plaster, with a slim ink moulding, a wide warm mat, a hairline bevel and a soft natural shadow. Below it sits a museum label in Cormorant with one tiny red dot, the only accent, sampled from the ruby. The upper two thirds is one calm object; the lower third is air and three lines of type.
concepts.why_clicks: H18 is the best-converting single photo in the account: E2 fruit plate Story, 4.32% CTR on 20,253 impressions, 24 purchases at 2.27x. Its ancestor ‘Anaar, pre-peeled.’ ran at 5.49% with 15 sales at 3.63x. A red sold dot is instantly legible and makes people want to see what is still available. ‘Gone to a good home’ is warm and wry rather than salesy.
concepts.shop_all_logic: The hero is explicitly unavailable, so the only action left is the rest of the shop: ‘The rest of the collection is still on view. From ₹599.’ The museum framing implies a gallery with more rooms to walk through.

concepts.name: Left ear, right ear
concepts.idea: A mirrored diptych of the store’s own on-model photos. Her left profile wears the Emerald Deco Hoops and her right profile wears the Pearl Nugget Hoops, set back to back so the two ears meet at the gutter like a reflection that refused to match. Headline: “Left ear, right ear.” Line: “Nobody said they had to match.” The offer is the twist: any two, 10% off.
concepts.why_beautiful: Two equal panels, one warm beige ground, mustard straps and dark hair framing a perfectly symmetrical composition, with the green and the pearl sitting at the same height either side of a 24px gutter. The catalogue photos are cropped tight to the ear and jaw so they look like a portrait series, not a listing. The type is centred, quiet and short.
concepts.why_clicks: These are the on-model listing photos that the Bestsellers catalogue carousel is built on (5.73% CTR, 43 purchases at 2.67x in 14 days, the account’s best purchase driver). ‘Show many pieces, on her’ is a proven converter. The mismatch is a small, stylish surprise that makes people look twice. It turns the Buy 2 offer into a styling idea instead of a discount shout, keeping the offer low in the hierarchy as the research advises.
concepts.shop_all_logic: Two different products are presented as one look, which invites people to pair their own from the whole collection. ‘Any two: 10% off, applied in your bag’ is a reason to open the full shop and pick two, from any category.

concepts.name: Haiku, in three pieces
concepts.idea: A real 5-7-5 haiku, set like a poem on the empty blush wall above the ruby necklace and anaar: “Rangoli, for ears. / Elaichi, around the wrist. / Anaar, at the throat.” Each line names a familiar Indian thing in the colour of one Naira piece: the rangoli studs, the elaichi-green bracelet, and the anaar-red necklace pictured. ‘In three pieces’ is the pun: it is a poem in three lines and an edit of three pieces.
concepts.why_beautiful: One photo, full bleed, with its own vast calm wall used as the page. The poem is set in centred Cormorant italic like a printed verse, with a tiny gold tag above it. The necklace, the neck form and the halved pomegranate sit untouched in the lower two thirds. It looks like a page from a book of poems that happens to sell jewellery.
concepts.why_clicks: H06 is the successor of ‘Anaar, pre-peeled.’ (5.49% CTR, 15 sales at 3.63x). The brand’s winning device, a familiar Indian thing in the stone’s colour, is used three times in one breath: rangoli (‘Rangoli you can wear.’ 5.21% on these studs, ‘Rangoli, in a line.’ 6.10%), elaichi and anaar. Only the last line is pictured, so the first two make people curious to see the rangoli earrings and the elaichi bracelet. No Indian jewellery brand runs a haiku.
concepts.shop_all_logic: Three categories (ears, wrist, throat) form a curated edit, and only one is shown. ‘Three pieces of a much longer poem.’ frames the whole collection as the rest of the poem, with the range ₹599 to ₹2,399.

The stripes stop the thumb on colour alone. The ‘onwards’ pun, a figure numbering joke and the price idiom every Indian shopper knows (‘₹599 onwards’), is the quiet smile that earns the tap. No Indian jewellery brand runs a book-figure ad.
concepts.shop_all_logic: Labelling the hero ‘Fig. 1’ declares it the first of many. ‘Fig. 2 onwards’ promises the rest of the book and names it (rings, earrings, necklaces, bracelets) with the entry price, ₹599 onwards.

risks: The pun depends on the second ‘onwards’. If the foot line wraps or is cut, the joke dies; keep it on one line.
H02’s stripes were the backdrop of the first ten’s ‘Rangoli, sorted by price’. This is a new treatment (a single printed plate with a figure caption), but avoid pairing the two in one flight.
The book framing can feel cool or academic. The warm paper and the colour of the plate must carry the warmth; do not use pure white.
An editorial lens may also build a book-page idea; the ‘Fig. 2 onwards’ line is what sets this one apart.

scores.notes: The strongest shop-all idea here. The crop works: H08 at 1.0x leaves calm linen above (0-333) and below (1100-1350), and the cover-price joke is earned. One thing: a 300px logo is too small to read as a masthead, so the title has to carry the cover. Set 'The Everything Issue' bigger (88-96px, across two lines if needed) and lose one hairline so it reads as a cover, not a form header. Risk, not fatal: fake covers are a Canva trope, so the craft has to be perfect. NOVEMBER 2026 expires on 30 Nov.

'Sold. The rest are on view.' is the clearest honest use of H18 and the founder's own seed. The deep wall will stand out in a cream feed. One thing: replace the CSS gilt gradient moulding and the drop-shadowed label card with a flat thin moulding and a label set straight on the wall. Gradient gilt reads as clip-art and kills the luxury. Also grow the frame so the bracelet is above 500px wide; at 0.33x it is small. Run only one sold-dot ad: this one, or a hybrid with MI3's simpler frame.

The diptych looks good when rendered: lips at the top of both tiles, chain and Prism bracelet, a real magazine page. 'Everything else, from ₹599.' is a fine turn. Weak spot: the mustard slip is only a sliver in the right tile and a band in the left, so the headline points at something you barely see. Most viewers will not know the 'model's own' credit idiom either. One thing: crop both tiles lower so the slip is clearly in frame, or pick two worn shots with more slip. It also looks close to the Bestsellers catalogue carousel she has already seen.

'Come in.' plus the meaning of a rangoli at the threshold is a lovely, true idea, and the hard-edged poster band is clean. In the Feed the rangoli is only the bottom ~240px, so the frame is mostly a teak step and a forearm, and the bracelet is about 200px. The Story, with the flower filling the lower half, is the better ad. One thing: cut 'OPEN ALL NIGHT'. It is filler and reads as a physical store. Keep 'ADMISSION FREE. SHIPPING TOO.' alone, right-aligned. H03 already ran in Diwali 10.

The type craft is nice (leaders, gold roman numerals, old-style figures), but it is still a list with about 16 text items, and the first ten already had one. The joke only lands if she reads the footnote. Prices without the ₹ sign break the brief's price rule (forgivable for the gag), and that is three prices plus a floor. Fatal in context: MI5 uses the same H06 wall with three lines of poem and does it better. Only keep this if MI5 dies.

A pretty still life with a pun almost nobody will catch. 'COLOPHON' is an obscure word, and three or four centred lines of 30px body copy read like small print at phone size. It will not stop a thumb, and H16 has the weakest proof of the six. One thing, if it is kept: cut to the gold label, 'Set in gold tone.' and a single line, 'Rings, earrings, necklaces, bracelets. ₹599 to ₹2,399.'

Fatal: a full-bleed, gorgeous sold-out bracelet with a 22px 'SOLD OUT' label is in effect an ad for a piece she cannot buy. Many will click for it and bounce, which breaks the spirit of H18's rule. The headline also fights the photo: a half anaar sits in the frame unfinished, and the line nods at food being eaten. The struck-through chip is product-page UI, not editorial. ED2/MI3 handle H18 honestly. Drop.

When rendered, #6E6627 reads drab and army-surplus on a phone, not 'cardamom'. The crops themselves are clean and the clasp survives. 'Elaichi, in a row.' is a retread of 'Rangoli, in a line.', and the running head, the 'Also rhyming' line and the footer pile three extra lines on a quiet idea. Only part of the bracelet shows. One thing: drop the olive ground and set the diptych on H11's own cream plaster, with just the headline and one breadth line.

The pet-names idea is warm, but 14 labels and five flat colour slabs make a paint-company template, the opposite of the brief's one-image restraint. Half the frame is flat colour, not jewellery. H02 already carried the first ten's C02. 'Kesar' for gold-tone hoops is a stretch. One thing, if revived: three chips at most, each beside a real crop of its piece, with no formal-name caps.

'Hang at ear height.' is the best single piece of wit in the batch, and the H08 window crop is lovely. But a cream mat centred on a peach wall is the stock Etsy framed-print mockup, low in contrast and slow in the feed. It sells one pair of hoops; the whole shop is one small italic line. One thing: harvest the line. It could be ED1's cover line, or the wall text on the ED2/MI3 gallery, instead of running as its own ad.

The three macro crops are genuinely beautiful when rendered (twisted huggie, knot, pavé link), and the craft verbs are on-brand. But a label column with three-line stacks beside three letterbox bands reads as a catalogue ledger, and 'Hooked?' is a groan. One thing: make it a true triptych of three equal verticals, only 'Twisted. Knotted. Linked.' under them, and close with 'The gold-tone edit. From ₹599.' Drop the per-piece names and prices.

The crop is mostly neck and skin, with an earring about 85x145px, so the jewel does not carry the frame. Then a caption, headline, two swatch circles with labels, two lines of body, a hairline and a footer pile up under it. 'Whatever you're wearing, the collection has its match' is a line that could sell anything, which the brief's own data says fails. The haldi swatch comes from a different photo. 'Haldi, meet aasmani.' is charming, but not enough.

The best thumb-stop of the 18. The rendered crop is cinematic: braided gold in a palm against amber bokeh, and a warm-black letterbox that will stand out in a cream feed. Subtitles get read by reflex, and 'Where's the rest?' asks the Shop All question for her. One thing: in the Story, replace the H13 reverse shot. Its red playing cards and green baize echo the first ten's Teen patti. Use a tighter second H07 band (fingers and hoops) or crop H13 to hand and ring only. Keep 'Cute.' light, and keep the subtitles 50px or larger.

The most beautiful single image here: the pavé link fills the frame, razor-sharp and downscaled, with the cream corner as a natural page. The idiom twist is quiet and clever. Weak spot: shop-all rests on small lines, and the Feed says the category breadth twice (caps line under the headline plus the bottom line). One thing: drop the top caps line and make the bottom 'The whole collection, ₹599 to ₹2,399.' the single, slightly larger breadth line. Check the bottom-left type against the link's cast shadows.

Honest and easy to build well (the mock shows a clean ink frame), but blush wall, blush mat and blush photo make it the quietest gallery option, and the bracelet is about 300px. 'Gone to a good home.' is warm but can read as pet rehoming. It duplicates ED2, so run only one. Best hybrid: MI3's simple ink frame and blush wall carrying ED2's line 'Sold. The rest are on view.', with the frame enlarged.

When rendered it reads instantly: mirrored ears meeting at the gutter, emerald with silver tone against pearl with gold tone, so the mismatch looks deliberate. The orientation is correct (left ear left, right ear right). The offer as a styling twist is exactly where the brief wants it. Weak spots: the 1.0x crops are skin-heavy and a touch clinical, and it shows only earrings. One thing: add 'from ₹599' to the offer line ('ANY TWO, FROM ₹599: 10% OFF IN YOUR BAG' or similar) so the shop beyond earrings is implied. Copy must never name the pearl's material; if it does, it must say shell pearl.

A true 5-7-5 that turns the house formula (Indian thing in the stone's colour) into three categories in one breath, set on H06's own wall with the photo untouched. That is real editorial beauty and the freshest idea in the set. Weak spot: it is quiet, and it explains itself twice (the HAIKU tag plus 'Three pieces of a much longer poem.'). One thing: keep the bottom line and shrink or drop the tag so the poem stands alone at the top. Check that the Story's stretched top band shows no seam.

The plate renders beautifully: the most graphic picture in the pool, at 0.504x, with the bracelet edge to edge across the stripes. It is the cleanest build in the set. But H02 carried the first ten's C02, the caption reuses the already-run 6.10% line, and the double 'onwards' is clunky on one long 32px line. One thing: shorten the foot to 'Fig. 2 onwards: the rest of the collection, ₹599 onwards.' so the pun has room. Do not run it beside another book conceit (ED5/ED6).

The proven H08 runs full-bleed at 1.0x and the copy names the categories and the price range, so the shop-all job is done. Better: the logo is capped at 300px, so the masthead is too small to read as a cover at phone size. Make 'The Everything Issue' the big element (96px or more) and give it more air above the hoop. The 22px dateline price joke will not be read in half a second. Check that the type stays legible on the folded, mottled linen in the top 300px. No fatal flaw.

This is the best of the three sold-dot ideas. The deep anaar wall stands out in a light feed, 'Sold.' is honest and stops the scroll, and the bracelet has nowhere to go except the rest of the shop. It follows the H18 rule exactly. Better: replace the gilt gradient moulding with a flat gold keyline or a thin dark moulding, because a gradient reads as plastic. Keep the window at least 488px wide. Build only this one of ED2, MI3 and CO1.

'Slip, model's own. Everything else, from ₹599.' is the best shop-all line in the batch. The visual is weak: two lip-cropped faces side by side read as catalogue tiles, close to the first ten's on-model grid (Solah shringar). Better: put the line on one dominant on-model crop, such as the Bold Nocturne Chain at collarbone height, instead of a diptych. The 232px bracelet tile is the weak jewel.

A rangoli at the threshold meaning 'Come in.' is a real cultural insight, it is timed to Diwali without saying Diwali, and the line is the shop-all invitation. The poster band with the hard edge looks expensive. Better: the bracelet is only about 205px wide. Shift the photo window down about 50px (source y 520-1440) so more rangoli petals show and the wrist sits on the upper third. Swap 'OPEN ALL NIGHT' for 'OPEN ALL HOURS' so nobody looks for a store.

Fatal: it is a priced list, the format family the first ten already used (Kisko kya, sorted by price, the price sum). The joke needs a footnote to explain it, so it fails at half a second. About 16 text items over the top 40% of the frame break the little-text bar. Rangoli and Pheni are not pictured. If H06 is used, MI5 uses the same wall better.

This is the pretty-but-sleepy type that loses. The pun will go unnoticed, it has the most body copy in the batch, and H16 has the weakest proof (3.90%). The Story strip under the photo must be feathered in seamlessly, which is a build risk. The fix is not small: it would need a single, louder line in place of a colophon paragraph.

Fatal: a full-bleed, buyable-looking hero that is sold out, explained only by a 22px label at the foot. That falls short of the pool.json 'say so plainly' rule, and clicks will come from people who want the ruby bracelet. The headline also contradicts the photo, because half the anaar is visibly still there, and 'finished' reads as eating. ED2 does this honestly.

The mocked crops work and the emerald pops, but the olive ground plus olive pods reads drab and muddy on a phone. The rhyme is weak: dull pods against bright stones, and the pods are a heap, not a row. 'Elaichi' was already a label in the first ten's masala dabba. 'Also rhyming: anaar, mishri, rangoli' is a clunky way to sell the whole shop. Better: a cream ground and a plain breadth line, but it would still be a second-tier idea.

Flat colour chips do stop the thumb, and the founder suggested a colour chart. But naming pieces after Indian things repeats the masala dabba and Haldi/Mehendi devices from the first ten. The window is H02 again (used in C02). The five chips stand for pieces she cannot see, and 14 labels is busy. Better: cut it to 3 chips, each with a small photo crop of its piece, and drop the words-only chips.

'Hang at ear height.' is a lovely one-read line. But a peach mat on a peach wall is low contrast and quiet in a feed. It reads as a single-product ad, and the shop sits in a whisper. It also overlaps ED2's gallery frame and ED1's photo, so run at most one of the three. Better: a darker wall sampled from the persimmon's shadow, for contrast.

Fatal: three stacked horizontal strips with prices down one side, including the Kiss Knot Bangle, is the first ten's 'Nobody wears one choodi' (C18) format. A monochrome cream-and-gold layout is also quiet in a feed. 'Hooked?' is weak, and these macros have no ad CTR of their own.

The 85x145px earring is lost in a 920x860 crop of skin, so there is nothing to stop on. 'Haldi' was already a label in the first ten (C17). The pairing is with a slip Naira does not sell, and 'Whatever you're wearing, the collection has its match' is the kind of generic line that has failed for this account. Better: a tight ear crop like MI4's.

People read subtitles by reflex, gold glows on black, the proven H07 crop works, and 'Where's the rest?' asks the shop-all question for her. Better: in the Story, H13's band shows a red card edge and a blurred hand of cards, which echoes Teen patti. Move the band down to about source y 1150-1550, or use a second, tighter H07 band. Keep the subtitles at 50px and keep 'Cute.' light so it does not sound ungrateful.

This is the most beautiful frame in the batch: a full-frame pavé macro is a real thumb-stop, and the crops check out with clean cream top-left. Its weakness is shop-all, because it reads as a chain ad. Better: set the breadth line right under the headline in the Story too, so 'another' visibly means more pieces. Check the bottom-left credit for link shadow and nudge the crop up 20-40px if a letter crosses an edge. Never upscale.

It is honest and well made, and 'Gone to a good home' is warm. But the mock shows blush on blush with the lower third empty, which is sleepy next to ED2's anaar wall. The shop-all promise sits only in the whisper. Use it only as a fallback if ED2 fails the review. Never run two sold-dot ads.

The mirrored ears with mismatched hoops are graphic and surprising at phone size, the line is short and stylish, and Buy 2 works as the twist rather than a shout. The crop preview is ready. Better: only earrings are shown, so add the breadth ('Rings, earrings, necklaces, bracelets · from ₹599') after the offer, or write 'ANY TWO PIECES'. Consider trimming each panel about 80px at the bottom, where the neck is just skin. Both pieces appeared in C17, but the treatment is new.

The calmest use of H06: the 5-7-5 count is correct, and 'in three pieces' sells the idea of an edit. But a top made of text reads as a poem before it reads as jewellery, so the stop is soft. Elaichi and anaar names echo the masala dabba. The Story's 170px top extension is a seam risk. Better: drop the 'HAIKU, IN THREE PIECES' tag and let the poem plus 'Three pieces of a much longer poem.' carry it. Run only one of MI5 and ED5.

It is clean and the stripes stop the thumb on colour. But it is the same photo and nearly the same composition as C02 in the first ten (the bracelet across the stripes), so retargeted viewers will see a repeat. The 'onwards' pun sits in a 32px foot line, at the bottom of the hierarchy. Better: make the foot line the second-biggest type. Pick at most one of ED4 and MI6 for the Prism slot, and ED4 is stronger.

Best of the three H18 sold-out ideas. Run this one only and drop CO1 and MI3. I mocked it up: the crop (x180-1682, y300-2235 at 0.325x) matches the 488x629 window exactly, the bracelet comes out about 430px wide and the pomegranate enters top-right. Against the anaar wall it looks rich and gallery-like. The label meets the H18 rule exactly: 'Ruby red', 'Gold tone, cubic zirconia', a red dot with SOLD, no price, and the founder's own seed line. One fix: in the Story, 'Sold.' at 140px over 'The rest are on view.' at 58px reads as 'everything is sold out' for half a second. Raise the second line to about 84px, or keep both on one line as in the Feed. Keep the gilt moulding thin and matte; a shiny 8px gradient will look like clip-art. No fatal flaw.

Crops verified against the 2048px close-up. In the Feed at 0.75x the pavé link lands at about x180-982, y412-952, with clean cream top-left and bottom-left. In the Story at 0.9375x the link spans the width, and the top-right plain link starts at x≈1003. It is never upscaled. The line works three ways: a chain link, a link you tap, and 'one thing leads to another'. Main fix: the breadth line 'RINGS · EARRINGS · NECKLACES · BRACELETS' (Jost 26px, .24em tracking) runs about 880-920px, so it ends near x 950-990, right where the top-right plain link starts (x≈988). Drop the tracking to .16em or 24px, and make the line visible enough that the shop meaning lands. Price ₹1,799 is correct (17 in stock). No fatal flaw.

H08 at 1.0x checked: the upper hoop's pin sits at frame y≈335 and the title's descender at about 288, a 45px gap that is tight but fine. The cover line sits on clean linen (luminance 121-241). Two fixes. (1) Honesty: the credit 'WOVEN GOLD HOOPS' in caps is exactly what round 1 flagged as reading like a gold material claim. Use 'WOVEN HOOPS, ₹1,199', as the first ten did. (2) The vertical credit at x 984-1000 runs through the persimmon's cast shadow (luminance drops to about 54), so start it lower or check its contrast on the render. Craft: a 300px logo is small for a masthead, so the 'cover' depends on the hairline dateline and title. Make the italic title the hero (80-90px) so it reads as a cover and not as a poster. Range ₹599-2,399 and the categories are correct. Allowed because the masthead is NAIRA's own.

Plate preview checked: the full-width H02 at 0.504x is clean, graphic and warm on paper. (pool.json says the bracelet is in the upper third; it actually sits at about 47-54% of the height, and the spec's crop accounts for this.) Risk: the foot line 'Fig. 2 onwards: rings, earrings, necklaces, bracelets. ₹599 onwards.' at CGI 32px is about 68 characters, roughly 870px, inside a 936px measure. It is one wrap away from killing the pun, so set it at 30px, or make it 'Fig. 2 onwards: the rest, ₹599 onwards.' The prices are correct (₹2,399, ₹599). It reuses H02 (first ten C02) and the account's own old line, 'Rangoli, in a line.'. That is allowed, but never run it in the same flight as C02, and it may tire a retargeted audience.

Mocked up all three macros: the twisted huggie, the knot and the pavé link look like one luxurious shoot at 0.31-0.5x, all sharp and all downscaled. The craft words are true (torsade means twist, plus knot and link). Exactly three prices, the maximum, all correct (₹1,199, ₹1,199, ₹1,799). Fix: the Bold Nocturne crop (y700-1660) puts the top of the pavé link only about 10px under the panel edge, so move it to about y640-1600. Risk: three stacked horizontal photo bands with prices beside them look like the first ten's 'Nobody wears one choodi' layout. Keep it cream and umber, with no '+' or '=' anywhere. The 'Hooked?' payoff is the weakest beat, and a monochrome page stops less than colour.

I mocked up the diptych and it reads like a real fashion page; the chain and bracelet are both sharp. But the joke's object is missing on the right: the Prism Rivière crop (x250-805, y120-1045) shows almost no mustard slip (a sliver bottom-right), and the lips sit on the tile's left edge (x≈6) while the left tile's lips are centred. Fix: re-crop so the slip strap or neckline is visible in both tiles and the lips sit at similar positions, or swap the right tile for kiss-knot-bangle-worn (strap and wrist both in frame). 'Model's own' is a credit idiom on styled listing photos, not a factual claim; keep 'Slip, not for sale.' as the fallback. Prices correct (₹1,799, ₹2,399).

I mocked up the crop: at 1.0x the bracelet lands at frame y≈513-732, only about 80px under the hard band edge, and the forearm comes straight out of the band line. It feels cramped against the type block. Weak point: 'Come in.' on its own is close to the generic lines that failed (lesson 6). The meaning of rangoli at the door has to be on the page, for example 'The rangoli's done. Come in.' 'OPEN ALL NIGHT' can read as a physical store; use 'OPEN ALL HOURS'. 'Admission free. Shipping too.' is true (free insured shipping). H03 already ran as Diwali 10 ad 02.

Verified 5-7-5. Each line maps to a real in-stock piece: Prism Cluster Studs ('Rangoli you can wear.' 5.21%), the emerald tennis bracelet (₹1,499) and the ruby necklace pictured (₹2,099). The H06 wall is clean for type (luminance 185-222). Calm and beautiful, but the stop is moderate: it is a poem on a quiet photo, and two of the three pieces are not shown. It uses the same photo and wall as ED5; build at most one (this is the prettier one, ED5 sells harder). Story: stretching four rows over 170px will streak. Use a flat fill sampled from the wall plus grain, or skip the shift, since the poem fits y 290-700 on the native wall.

Strongest whole-shop logic of the H06 pair, and the wall is verified even for type (luminance 185-222). Prices map correctly: Anaar = ruby necklace ₹2,099, Rangoli = Prism Rivière ₹2,399, Pheni = Silk Mesh Cuff ₹1,399 (only 10 left in gold tone on H05). But the folios drop the ₹ sign by design, which the brief asks for, and only the footnote rescues it. About 16 text pieces push past the 12% text bar, and a list with dot leaders is close to the banned 'list' format (Kisko kya). Fix: cut the roman numerals and the running head, keep three entries plus 'Everything else', and make the footnote the second thing the eye reads. Rangoli and Pheni are unpictured, so cold audiences get no payoff.

Mocked up the mat window (0.625x): it looks lovely, with the hoops about 225px each and the persimmon centred. But it is pale on pale (peach wall, cream mat, peach linen), so it will not stop a thumb, and the whole-shop job rests on one italic line. Honesty fix: 'WOVEN GOLD HOOPS · ₹1,199' in caps reads as a gold claim, so use 'WOVEN HOOPS'. It uses the same photo as ED1 and the same framed-print device as ED2 and MI3. Run at most one framed print and one H08 ad. Persimmon gives no Indian turn.

This is a solid sold-dot ad that ED2 beats on every count. The bracelet is smaller here (about 375px at 0.28x), the blush wall with ink moulding is less striking than the anaar wall, and only one sold-dot ad can run. Honesty fix if it is ever used: the title 'Ruby, with anaar' uses 'Ruby' as a noun and reads as a gemstone claim. It must be 'Ruby red, with anaar'. Otherwise it meets the H18 rule (SOLD plus a red dot, no price).

Every fact is true (silver tone, cubic zirconia, ₹599-2,399, gift box, free insured 3-5 days). But this has the lowest thumb-stop of the 18: pale plaster, a pale envelope and three or four lines of body copy, and the typographer's pun will pass most people by. The Feed plaster under the envelope is clean enough for the block. In the Story, the flat fill under the photo meets a sunlight patch on the right edge (source x 1000+, y 1700-1900), so a seam will show unless that patch is cloned out first. Fix: cut the body to two lines and set 'Set in gold tone.' much larger, so the single line does the stopping.

Crop previews checked: the letterboxed H07 band is cinematic and the hoops are big. The problem is tone. A man hands her a gift and she answers 'Cute. Where's the rest?'. That reads as entitled, not as a sharp friend, and it cuts against the self-purchase audience. In the Story her reverse shot wears the solitaire-look Cushion Halo Ring, which reads as an engagement-ring 'upgrade'. Still 2 is also the H13 card table, which echoes the first ten's Teen patti. Fix: give her a self-purchase reply, such as '– Cute. I'll get the rest myself.', and use a second, tighter H07 band instead of H13.

Mocked up with the specified chips: five flat chips take about 40% of the frame, and the saturated ruby and emerald blocks fight the pastel H02 window. Only one piece of jewellery is shown, so the 'colour index' is abstract, and 14 labels break the little-text bar. 'Kesar' (saffron) for gold tone is a stretch. 'Jamuni · lilac huggies' depends on the Amethyst variant within 42 units across four colours, so check stock. H02 again (first ten C02). Fix: narrow the strip to about 160px so the photo dominates, and cut the formal-name labels.

Opened the planner's crop preview mi4_feed_crop.jpg: both panels are mostly neck skin, the tops of both ears are cut off, and each hoop is about 120px. It looks clinical rather than editorial. The hoops do sit level (emerald y≈345-555, pearl y≈350-545), so the mirror works. The copy is good, and the offer as the twist is true ('Buy 2, get 10% off', applied in the bag). Only earrings are shown. Keep it to the product name 'Pearl Nugget Hoops' (shell pearl, never freshwater). Fix: crop from higher and wider so the whole ear, the jawline and more hair at the gutter are in frame, making it read as a portrait pair.

I mocked up the 920x860 panel: it is mostly neck and shoulder skin with an earring about 85x145px, so the jewel is a glint and the haldi is a thin strap. The swatch circles do more work than the product. 'Whatever you're wearing, the collection has its match' is a generic promise that could sell anything. The colours check out: slip median #D7892E against the spec's #CF8027, heart stone #8092A9 against #88A2BA. Facts are fine (₹1,499, silver tone).

Fatal on the H18 rule. The sold-out bracelet is the full-bleed hero at 0.586x and looks buyable. The only 'sold out' is a 22px label at the bottom, which is not saying it plainly. 'RUBY BRACELET' implies a ruby gemstone and must be 'RUBY RED'. 'Someone finished the anaar' points to eating food while a whole anaar sits in the frame, so the joke takes two steps. The crop geometry checks out (headline clear of the pomegranate, chip 34px under the lowest aril). ED2 does the same job honestly and more beautifully.

Both crops verified: the left shows the cardamom heap with split pods, the right the lower strand of baguettes with the clasp in frame, both at about 0.58x. But the rhyme is weak: pale olive pods against deep emerald baguettes lack the exact colour match that made 'Rangoli, in a line.' click. The olive #6E6627 ground will look muddy on phones. It is the weakest whole-shop ad: one product, plus a text line about rhymes that are not shown. Elaichi was also a label in the first ten's masala dabba.

reserve: MI3 (as a hybrid): only if A02 fails review. Use MI3's simple 8px ink moulding on the blush wall, carrying ED2's line 'Sold. The rest are on view.', with the frame enlarged so the bracelet is 480px or wider, and the label 'Ruby red, with anaar' (never 'Ruby, with anaar'). Never run two sold-dot ads.

ED5 trimmed: only if A07 fails, since they share H06's wall and can never run together. Cut the roman numerals and the running head, keep 'Contents' with Anaar 2,099 / Rangoli 2,399 / Pheni 1,399 / Everything else from 599, and make 'Page numbers are prices.' the second thing the eye reads (32px or more).

CO3 cut to three chips: if a colour chart is wanted. Use three chips at most (Anaar, Elaichi, Mishri), each beside a real crop of its own piece, with no formal-name caps and the H02 window dropped. Risk: Indian-name labels echo the first ten's masala dabba and Haldi/Mehendi tiles.

dropped.why: Fatal for two judges and unfixed. A full-bleed, buyable-looking sold-out bracelet explained only by a 22px label breaks the spirit of H18's 'say so plainly' rule, and 'Someone finished the anaar' reads as food being eaten next to a whole anaar. A02 does the H18 job honestly.

The lowest buyer and art director scores among the rest. The olive #6E6627 ground renders drab on phones, the pod-to-emerald rhyme is weak, 'Elaichi' was already a masala-dabba label, and the 'Also rhyming' line sells rhymes that are not shown.

Lowest combined score (6.06). The earring is about 85x145px in a frame of neck skin, the swatches outwork the product, 'Haldi' repeats C17, and 'Whatever you're wearing, the collection has its match' is the kind of line that could sell anything.
